passage:
Monday. Preeti came out of the placement interview knowing she'd fumbled the database question. On the auto ride back she built it: no offer today, so no offer this season, so no job at all. Mummy and Papa had taken a loan for her fees. She pictured telling relatives at Diwali that she was still 'looking', year after year. The thought felt as solid as maths.
Wednesday. Vijay, her lab partner, sat with her in the library and asked, 'How many companies are left on the list?' She counted: fourteen. 'And how many rounds did you clear on Monday?' Two out of three.
Saturday. Preeti printed the list and ticked three companies. She revised databases for an hour and then, for the first time that week, went to sleep before midnight.

qa.q: How many companies were still left on the placement list?
qa.a: Fourteen companies were left on the list.

qa.q: Why did the chain from one interview to 'no job at all' feel as solid as maths to Preeti?
qa.a: Each step followed neatly from the last, and her guilt about the fee loan made the worst ending feel deserved, so she never noticed the steps she skipped, like the other companies and the rounds she cleared.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Preeti's week?
qa.a: Vijay's plain questions about companies left and rounds cleared turned a feeling into numbers, and by Saturday Preeti had a ticked list and revision time instead of a spiral.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Preeti's Monday reaction?
qa.a: Vijay could see she had cleared two of three rounds, a fact the fear was hiding, so Vijay asked questions rather than arguing to help her count what was real.

grounding: Shows a final-year student leaping from one weak interview to never finding work and family shame, then steadying over a week.

passage: Wasim, you've been staring at that rejection mail since lunch. Let me tell you about my own final year. I failed my first interview at a bank. Froze on a question about interest rates I'd answered a hundred times in class. On the train home I had my whole life decided. No bank would take me. No company either, once word got around. My father had retired early to pay my college fees, and I saw him at every wedding explaining that his son was sitting at home. I didn't eat dinner. I truly believed it was plain reasoning. Your Dadi, my mother, just put a plate in front of me and said, 'One interview, Suraj. You're counting it like it's the last one.' I got my first job four months later. Not a bank. It was fine.

qa.q: What question made Suraj freeze in his first interview?
qa.a: A question about interest rates that Suraj had answered a hundred times in class.

qa.q: Why did Suraj skip dinner that night?
qa.a: Suraj believed his chain of thoughts was plain reasoning, and the picture of his father explaining at weddings filled him with shame, so the future felt already lost.

qa.q: Which line from Dadi changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: 'You're counting it like it's the last one' showed that one interview was being treated as the whole future, which let Suraj see the many steps he had skipped.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel hearing this story from Suraj?
qa.a: Wasim may feel less alone and the rejection may feel less final, since someone older once felt the same and still found work four months later.

grounding: Shows an older relative recalling how, in his final year, one failed interview became in his mind a life without work and his father's shame.

passage: The power had been out in Ladies' Hostel B since six, and Alka's phone was at nine percent when the email came: 'We regret to inform you...' It was the one company she'd really wanted. In the candle-lit room her mind raced ahead. Not selected here means not selected anywhere. Twenty-two and unemployed. Her mother telling the neighbours she was 'preparing for something'. Her younger brother getting a job before her. It felt like reasoning, not panic. Jasleen, her roommate, held up the candle. 'Read me the next line.' Alka read: 'We will keep your profile for future openings.' Then the phone died. In the dark, Jasleen said, 'That's one company on one Tuesday. Tomorrow the power's back and there are twelve more on the board.'

qa.q: What did the next line of the email say?
qa.a: It said, 'We will keep your profile for future openings.'

qa.q: Why did Alka's leap from one rejection to being unemployed feel like reasoning?
qa.a: Each step seemed to follow from the one before, and the dark room with a dying phone left nothing else to look at; worry about her mother and younger brother made the chain feel heavy and true.

qa.q: What small step helped stop Alka's spiral?
qa.a: Jasleen asked Alka to read the next line, which added a real fact the fear had skipped, and then named the plain truth: one company, twelve more on the board.

qa.q: If you were Jasleen holding the candle, what would you want Alka to notice?
qa.a: Jasleen would want Alka to see how much of the story was guessed, and that the next day would bring light, a charged phone and more chances.

grounding: Shows a final-year student in a power cut jumping from one rejection to lifelong unemployment and family shame, until a roommate points back to the facts.

passage:
The group discussion round at the Lucknow campus had lasted twelve minutes, and Reena had spoken for maybe forty seconds. When the list went up, her roll number wasn't on it.

On the walk to the metro, her mind moved fast. If I can't pass a group discussion, I can't pass anything. Every company has one. So no job this year. Then everyone gets placed but me. Papa will stop mentioning me to his friends. Chachi will ask at every wedding. I'll be twenty-five and still at home, filling forms.

It felt like a perfectly logical chain.

Yusuf caught up with her at the ticket gate. "You okay? That was just the first company."

"It's not about one company," Reena said. "It's about what it shows."

"What does it show?"

She opened her mouth and realised she couldn't answer without jumping straight to the wedding.

qa.q: For how long had Reena spoken in the group discussion?
qa.a: Reena had spoken for maybe forty seconds.

qa.q: Why does Reena's chain of thoughts feel logical to her?
qa.a: Each step sounds reasonable on its own, like "every company has one", so the leap to never being employed seems proven. The shame of not being on the list makes the worst ending feel likely.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the ticket gate, and what could Reena do next?
qa.a: Yusuf's simple question, "What does it show?", made her notice she had skipped straight to the wedding. Next she could write down the actual steps between one lost round and never being employed.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Reena's reaction to one list?
qa.a: Yusuf sees one company and one round, so Reena's sadness may seem bigger than the event. Yusuf seems to care enough to ask rather than argue.

grounding: A final-year student who missed one campus round pictures never getting a job and shaming her family, a chain that skips every step between.

passage:
Anand pushed the rice around his plate.

"How was the interview?" Disha asked. She had come home early from her office to hear.

"Gone. I blanked on the coding question."

"Okay. So that company's gone."

"Not just that company, Didi. If I blank there, I'll blank everywhere. Then no job. Then Baba takes that loan for nothing. Then I'm the son who sits at home while Rinku's son is in Bengaluru."

"Wait. You got from one question to Rinku's son in one breath."

"Because that's where it goes!"

"Is it? What happened between the question and 'no job'?"

Anand stopped. "...I don't know. It just feels like the same thing."

"How many companies are left on your list?"

"Nine."

Disha put a piece of fish on his plate. "Then that's nine chances to blank or not blank. Eat. Then show me the question."

He picked up his spoon, slowly.

qa.q: How many companies are left on Anand's list?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: Why does Anand say "Because that's where it goes!" when Disha points out his leap?
qa.a: To Anand the chain feels automatic, as if one blanked question already contains the whole unhappy future. The shame about Baba's loan makes the worst case feel more real than the steps in between.

qa.q: Which question of Disha's helped most, and why?
qa.a: "What happened between the question and 'no job'?" It made Anand look for the missing steps, and he admitted he didn't know, which loosened the chain.

qa.q: How might Disha feel hearing her brother call himself the son who sits at home?
qa.a: Disha may feel worried and protective, since she came home early to hear about the interview. She seems to want him to see his chances clearly rather than feel ashamed.

grounding: A final-year student who blanked in one interview imagines never getting a job and letting his father down, and his sister asks about the missing steps.

passage: The rejection email arrived while Zanele was queuing for a taxi outside the Braamfontein campus. Thank you for your interest. She read it three times on the ride home. By the time she climbed the stairs to the flat, the logic had built itself. If the engineering firm didn't want her, none of them would. Graduation would come with no job. She'd move back to Soweto and sit in her mother's lounge while the neighbours asked what all that studying had been for. Her little brother, who told everyone his sister would build bridges, would stop saying it. Kaito, her flatmate, found her sitting on the floor with her shoes still on. 'That's one company,' he said, handing her tea. 'How many applications have you still got open?' She counted, frowning. Seven. She hadn't thought of them once all the way home.

qa.q: How many applications did Zanele still have open?
qa.a: She still had seven applications open.

qa.q: Why did Zanele's chain from one rejection to living in shame feel logical to her?
qa.a: She was crushed and ashamed, and each picture seemed to follow from the one before, so she skipped the many steps in between, like the seven other applications.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Kaito's question offer?
qa.a: Asking how many applications were still open made her count real evidence, which interrupted the jump from one no to never being employed.

qa.q: How does Kaito see the rejection?
qa.a: Kaito sees it as one company's decision, not a verdict on her future, and he brings her back to the facts gently with tea and a question.

passage: The placement cell corridor still smelled of fresh paint. Irawati sat on the bench outside Room 4, where the panel had just thanked her and called the next name. She had frozen on the second question. Her mind was already running. Six companies were visiting this month and they all talked to each other, surely. Word would spread. Every panel would see a girl who froze. May would come, and her batchmates would post their offer letters while she stayed silent. Her father had told the whole village she would work in Bengaluru. She would have to go home and face him. Rukmini, the placement coordinator, stopped by the bench with a clipboard. 'Your aptitude score was the third best in the batch,' she said. 'Did you know that?' Irawati hadn't even looked.

qa.q: What happened to Irawati in Room 4?
qa.a: She froze on the second question, and the panel thanked her and called the next name.

qa.q: Why did Irawati believe every company would hear about her freezing?
qa.a: She was panicked and ashamed, so the idea that companies talk to each other felt obvious, and each fearful step seemed to prove the next.

qa.q: What could Irawati do to check the chain she had built?
qa.a: She could write down each step and ask what evidence supports it, starting from facts like her strong aptitude score and the other companies still visiting.

qa.q: What does Rukmini's comment show about how others see Irawati?
qa.a: Rukmini sees a strong candidate with the third-best aptitude score, not someone who is finished after one hard interview.

passage:
Subject: I think I've ruined everything

Hafsa di,
You said to write if placements got hard, so here I am at 2 a.m. The analytics firm rejected me today after the final round. I keep replaying it. If I couldn't crack the one company that matches my project, who will take me? I can already see June: everyone joining offices, me refreshing job sites at home. Amma has been telling the relatives that I'm 'almost settled'. She'll have to take that back at the next wedding. Appa won't say anything, which is worse. I know I'm jumping ahead, but it feels like I'm just being realistic. Tell me honestly, did this happen to anyone in your batch? Did they recover?
Sorry for the long mail.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How could Hafsa reply in a way that helps?

qa.q: How might Amma see the rejection if Jahnavi told her?
qa.a: Amma might see it as one company's no rather than a failure, and could care more about Jahnavi's worry than about what relatives say.

passage:
Deepika, don't laugh, but I have to say this out loud. I'm Tanuja, and today I failed the second-round interview with the logistics company. They said, "We'll go with other candidates."

And my brain went: if I can't clear this one, I can't clear any. Placement season ends in March. Everyone else will get jobs. I'll be the only one from our batch sitting at home. Papa took that loan for my fees. He'll have to tell the relatives. Mummy will stop going out because people will ask. I'll be twenty-five and still unemployed, and everyone will whisper.

It feels like maths, you know? One plus one plus one. But I've failed one interview. There are nine companies left on the list. I know that. It just doesn't feel like I know it.

qa.a: There are nine companies left on the list.

passage:
Before, Monday: Baljeet walked out of the bank's interview in Chandigarh sure he'd stumbled on the case question. By the bus stop the story was complete: no offer here, no offer anywhere, the family's savings spent on his degree for nothing, a lifetime of cousins asking, "Still no job?"

During, Wednesday: the rejection email came. Baljeet skipped lunch. He told Imran, "That's it. I'm unemployable." Imran asked, "How many companies are left this season?" "Twelve." "And how many have you failed?" "One." "So you're one-twelfth unemployable?" Baljeet didn't laugh, but his shoulders dropped a little.

After, the next Tuesday: Baljeet sat his next interview. He had practised the case question with Imran three times. He still didn't know if he'd got it, but on the bus back he noticed he was only thinking about dinner.

qa.q: How many companies were left this season?
qa.a: Twelve companies were left.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet say "I'm unemployable" after one rejection?
qa.a: Baljeet felt anxious and ashamed, and his mind leapt from one failed interview to a lifetime of shame, skipping all the steps between.

qa.a: Imran takes it seriously but sees the leaps, using gentle humour and numbers to bring it back to size.

passage:
Rukmini, you think one bad interview is the end? Sit. Your Tenzin uncle had one too. It was my final year in Darjeeling, and I failed the interview for a tea company in Siliguri. The manager said I spoke too softly.

On the jeep ride home, I ruined my whole life. No job, then my mother selling her earrings, then my younger brothers leaving school, then the whole village knowing Tenzin was a failure. By the time we reached Ghoom, I had practically buried myself.

Your grandfather listened to all of it that night. Then he asked one question: "And tomorrow morning, what will you do?" I said, "Practise speaking loudly." He said, "Good. Do that."

Three months later I got the job at the school. Still here, still speaking loudly.

qa.q: Why did the manager reject young Tenzin?
qa.a: The manager said he spoke too softly.

qa.q: What was young Tenzin feeling on the jeep ride home?
qa.a: Young Tenzin felt ashamed and anxious, picturing his whole family ruined because of one failed interview.

qa.q: What turning point in the story broke the spiral?
qa.a: His father's question, "And tomorrow morning, what will you do?", turned the dread into one concrete step: practising speaking loudly.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's father have felt listening to the whole spiral?
qa.a: He was probably worried but calm, choosing one practical question instead of arguing with every fear.

passage: Harish walked out of the placement cell at four, rejected after the second round. It was raining, his phone was on five percent, and the college bus had broken down, so he stood under the shed with forty other students. In his head it ran like a train. Failed this one. Won't get the next one. Batchmates will all be placed by March. I'll be home with no job. Amma will tell relatives I'm "still preparing". Appa will stop asking. I'll be twenty-five and still living in my old room. He felt sick. His phone buzzed: Simran. "How did it go?" He typed, "Failed. My life is finished." Two percent battery. She called. "Harish, stop. One interview. How many companies are left this season?" He counted. "Twenty-three." "So between one no and a finished life, there are twenty-three chances. Charge your phone and we'll list them." The bus arrived.

qa.q: How many companies were left this season?
qa.a: Twenty-three companies were left this season.

qa.q: Why did the chain of disasters feel like logic to Harish?
qa.a: Harish felt ashamed and anxious after the rejection, so each step seemed to follow from the last even though many steps were skipped.

qa.q: What did Simran do that helped?
qa.a: She asked a concrete question, how many companies were left, so Harish could see the gap between one no and a finished life.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt reading "My life is finished"?
qa.a: Simran was probably alarmed and worried, which is why she called at once instead of texting back.

passage: After the group discussion round, Manoj went straight back to the hostel room in Chennai and lay on his bed with his shoes on. He had spoken only twice. The panel hadn't even looked at him. By the time Shankar came in, Manoj had built the whole future. "That's it. I won't get placed. Off-campus is harder. I'll be unemployed for years. Appa sold the land for my fees, and I'll have wasted it. I can't even go home for Pongal and face them." Shankar pulled off Manoj's shoes and sat on the other bed. "Okay. Walk me through it. From one GD to unemployed for years. What's step two?" Manoj opened his mouth. "Step two is... the next company is on Monday." "And?" "And it's a written test first. I'm good at those." Shankar raised an eyebrow. "So your step two is a test you're good at." Manoj laughed, shakily, for the first time that evening.

passage:
It was the week before Christmas, placement season, and the campus was strung with fairy lights I couldn't stand to look at. I'd just come out of the first interview of the season, where I froze on the second coding question.
Walking back, my mind ran ahead like a train. They'll reject me. Then every company will. I'll be the only one in the batch without a job. Papa took a loan for my fees; I'll never repay it. Everyone at home will whisper. By the hostel gate I'd reached "failure at thirty".
Gopika found me on the steps. "Omkar, what happened?" I told her the whole chain. She said, "Okay. What actually happened in the last hour?"
"I froze on one question."
"And?"
Said out loud, the chain looked ridiculous. One interview. Twelve companies still to come.
